(EPA Images pic) BUDAPEST: Hungary's former nationalist Prime Minister Viktor Orban, who was ousted after 16 years in power in an election in April, has urged his supporters to restore democracy in the country which he said had been crushed by the new government. Orban made his first strong political statements since his landslide election defeat late on Tuesday on Facebook, issuing a "Statement of Resistance" shortly after his Fidesz party said prosecutors had raided offices housing its internet servers. Prosecutors told Reuters in an emailed response that the action was linked to an investigation into "misappropriation and other criminal offences" at the National Culture Fund (NKA) under Orban's government. Orban said that Hungary had "ceased to be a democratic state" after the new centre-right government of Prime Minister Peter Magyar passed a constitutional amendment ending the mandate of the president and the head of the constitutional court. Tisza denies taking an authoritarian stance towards political opponents. It has pledged to curb corruption, which it says was rampant under Orban's administration, part of Tisza's drive to bring Hungary back into the EU mainstream. Orban himself faced heavy criticism during his rule over democratic standards in Hungary, which was in frequent conflict with the EU over issues such as the rule of law and minority rights. Orban has denied the corruption allegations. "Again the age of tyranny started in Hungary," Orban said. "The new political system created this way is illegitimate...Fidesz will use all peaceful tools against abuse of power inside parliament and outside parliament." He will hold a press briefing at 0830 GMT. Magyar's Tisza party has a supermajority in ​parliament, which enables it to roll back changes introduced by Orban that Magyar says harmed democracy. The constitutional amendment ended President Tamas Sulyok's term, citing society's "serious loss of confidence" in a leader elected in 2024 by lawmakers from Orban's Fidesz party. Parliament will soon elect a new president. Magyar's Tisza commands huge public support, with a poll by pollster Median earlier this month showing 60% support, against 18% for Fidesz. Since the election, Fidesz has been in disarray, with its parliamentary group leader resigning last week.

Photograph: David McNew/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Dead trees are seen near Mammoth Lakes, California, in 2022. Photograph: David McNew/Getty Images US news Fossils show huge carbon emissions harm forests, not ‘green the planet’ Study of 56m-year-old leaves counters claims from Trump administration members of ‘benefits’ of fossil fuel pollution Oliver Milman Thu 13 Aug 2026 14.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Adding huge quantities of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere is set to cause the Earth’s forests to wither and die rather than flourish, according to a new study that counters erroneous claims that fossil fuel pollution will green the planet. An analysis of fossilized leaf cells from a period known as the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum (or PETM), which occurred about 56 million years ago, has helped reconstruct how the world’s forests responded when planet-heating gases were previously being released at a rapid rate. The current galloping pace of carbon emissions from the burning of fossil fuels is unmatched in historic and prehistoric records but the PETM, when huge amounts of carbon were released over a 130,000-year period and the world heated up by as much as 8C (14F), is the closest comparison. The authors of the new paper found this prehistoric change caused a retreat in the forests that blanketed the Paleocene-Eocene world, causing them to die off as the Earth browned rather than greened, a finding they state has “chilling implications” for today’s world. View image in fullscreen Fragments of fossilized leaves like these helped the authors recreate the forest canopies of 56m years ago. Photograph: Dr. Regan Dunn “What we see is that as the carbon dioxide ramped up, the forests became very dense but then subsequently collapsed, opening up dramatically,” said Regan Dunn, a researcher at La Brea Tar Pits and the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, who led the study. “Around 60% of the biomass of the standing vegetation was gone, it was a huge loss. This should be a concern because the rate of carbon release has never been higher than now.” Dun added: “Forests are some of our best friends and allies but we are already seeing them die back, be cut down and consumed by wildfires. It’s happening quickly, every summer the change seems faster and faster.” Trees may store less planet-heating carbon than hoped, study suggests Read more Plants like trees require carbon to build their structures and, along with water and sunlight, provide food. Once the world started to burn coal, oil and gas in huge volumes from the industrial revolution onwards, the amount of emitted carbon dioxide surged at an unprecedented rate, with atmospheric concentrations of CO 2 rising by more than 50% in little over a century. This increase in carbon did initially help boost some plant life, a change that has been seized upon by those who question the facts of climate science. Prominent figures in Donald Trump’s administration have argued that burning fossil fuels is good for the environment. “CO 2 was never a pollutant,” Doug Burgum, the interior secretary, told Fox Business earlier this year as the federal government moved to erase its own power to address the climate crisis. “When we breathe, we emit CO 2 . Plants need CO 2 to survive and grow. They thrive with more CO 2 .” On the same TV network last year, Chris Wright, Trump’s energy secretary, said that there were “pluses” to global heating as well as negatives. “A warmer planet with more CO 2 is better for growing plants,” Wright claimed. View image in fullscreen The authors compared the cuticle structure of modern leaves (pictured above under epifluorescence microscopy) with fossil leaf cuticles to create a model for canopy cover. Scale bar is 50 microns (0.05 mm). Photograph: Dr. Regan Dunn Experts have previously rejected such claims as false, with the new research paper, published in Science, showing that the Earth’s past experience demonstrates that trees require much more than CO 2 to thrive. Extra carbon dioxide traps more heat, causing trees to struggle amid extreme temperatures and a lack of key nutrients. Hotter conditions can also trigger outbreaks of pests and disease, weakening trees further, and dry out vegetation that then explodes into huge wildfires, such as those that have engulfed much of Canada and western Europe this summer. The switch from greening forests to browning forests occurred around 2000, the new paper states, when the impacts of drought and heat stress overtook the benefits of extra CO 2 . Since then, evidence has piled up of escalating global tree mortality, including trees in the tropics dying of dehydration. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Down to Earth The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential after newsletter promotion “Once the climate becomes too warm plants aren’t able to handle it, it affects their physiology and their relationship with water,” said Dunn. “Once they can’t survive because the CO 2 and temperatures are too high, that’s when you see forests die back.” There was “quite a lot of tree mortality” now occurring in Europe, North America and the Amazon, Dunn said, requiring swift cuts to carbon emissions to ensure that the world doesn’t barrel down the same path as it did 56m years ago. “There is still time to prevent the worst outcomes and best thing we can do is keep fossil fuels in the ground,” she said. “It’s important for people to understand that once we pass thresholds it takes a long time to recover from them. The 130,000 years of the PETM change on human timescales is basically forever.” Dunn and her colleagues ascertained the extent of ancient forests by analyzing fossilized cells of leaves called leaf cuticle fragments. This enabled them to ascertain the density of the forest canopy during the PETM, allowing them to calculate the advance and retreat of forests over time. View image in fullscreen The field crew excavating a trench through PETM strata in the Hanna Basin, Wyoming. Photograph: Marieke Dechesne, USGS In that past era, forests covered a much larger extent of the world than now, with no ice at the poles and much higher seas than today. But while the PETM changes occurred over many thousands of years via carbon released by the natural forces of volcanic activity, current climate change is much faster and caused by our deliberate combustion of fossil fuels. The paper is a “genuine advance” and provides a record over tens of thousands of years that shows the knock-on impacts of thinning forests, according to Trevor Keenan, a scientist at the University of California, Berkeley, who was not involved in the new research. “The headline is that warming won,” Keenan said. “Carbon dioxide rose sharply, and any benefit that gave the forests was not enough to stop canopies from opening up and staying open for tens of thousands of years.” This is worrying because the pace of change today, he added. “The ancient carbon release happened over thousands of years, ours is happening over decades,” he said. “Faster forcing gives ecosystems less room to adjust. “Second, those forests faced climate change alone. Today’s forests are dealing with the same warming while also being fragmented, logged, converted to agriculture and exposed to altered fire regimes. If forests thinned under the slower and cleaner version of this experiment, that is not a reassuring precedent.” Explore more on these topics US news Climate crisis Trees and forests Greenhouse gas emissions news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

A second suspected case of bird flu in the mammals has been found after the South Australian government confirmed the first case last week. Photograph: DEA/P. JACCOD/De Agostini/Getty Images Bird flu Australia has just 12,000 sea lions left – and ‘carnage’ may await them as bird flu takes hold, scientists warn Virus has already caused catastrophic losses in pinnipeds in South America and sub-Antarctica, particularly among pups Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Lisa Cox Environment and climate correspondent Mon 24 Aug 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 11.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Scientists have warned deadly H5 bird flu could cause “carnage” for Australia’s seal and sea lion populations after detection of the virus in long-nosed fur seals in South Australia . SA confirmed Australia’s first case in a mammal on Saturday after a dead long-nosed fur seal found at Beachport on the Limestone Coast tested positive for H5N1. The state government announced a second suspected case on Monday in a dead long-nosed fur seal found on the Pages Islands, off Kangaroo Island, with results from CSIRO testing pending. Leading mammal scientist John Woinarski, of Charles Darwin University, said he feared the virus would quickly start affecting more seals and sea lions. “The carnage may be substantial and represent a serious conservation impact,” he said. “I fear for Australian sea lions in particular because of their small population size. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email “It’s likely in the next few weeks it will spread more quickly into the sea lion population in South Australia generally because of the proximity of the sea lion colonies to breeding seabird colonies or affected seabirds.” H5 bird flu has already affected pinnipeds in South America and sub-Antarctica, where it has caused catastrophic losses in populations of some species, particularly among pups. In 2023, H5N1 killed more than 17,000 southern elephant seal pups in Argentina and drone surveys detected more than 13,000 dead southern elephant seal pups on Australia’s Heard Island in 2025 and 2026. Bird flu has devastated wildlife around the world. What Australian birds are most at risk? Read more “In South America, we’ve seen huge infection rates in sea lions and fur seals,” said Jane Younger, an Antarctic disease ecologist at the University of Tasmania. “Then across the Southern Ocean we’ve seen really big mortality rates in southern elephant seals and Antarctic fur seals. “In some places, the numbers are just astronomical.” Three types of pinnipeds breed in Australian waters – the long-nosed fur seal, the Australian fur seal and the endangered Australian sea lion. The Australian government has rated all at very high risk from H5 bird flu. Experts say about 12,000 Australian sea lions remain – though one recent estimate put the figure at less than 10,000 – with about three-quarters of the population found in South Australia and the remainder in Western Australia. Thousands of little penguins being vaccinated against H5 bird flu in Victoria – video The long-nosed fur seal suspected of having bird flu was found on the Pages Islands where, the SA government reported last week, there had been mass deaths among greater crested terns . The islands are home to one of Australia’s largest breeding colonies of Australian sea lions, with long-nosed fur seals known to visit the area. Younger said while there was some uncertainty about how Australia’s seals and sea lions would fare, the mortality rates seen in South America and the Southern Ocean “make me very worried”. “There’s only 12,000 Australian sea lions in existence,” she said. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “For some of these other species like elephant seals, we’ve seen many more than that killed by this virus. “Hopefully it doesn’t wipe out the species, but that’s a possibility.” Younger, said seals and sea lions were vulnerable to H5N1 because they gathered in large colonies that overlapped with seabirds infected with the virus. The environment itself, including the water and beaches, could also be contaminated with the virus. H5N1 can be transmitted from birds to seals or between seals. “At the moment there’s mass mortalities in birds and that infection will cause contamination of the environment,” said Rachael Gray, a pinniped specialist at the University of Sydney’s School of Veterinary Science. “Once you get mammals infected, it’s likely you will see mammal-to-mammal transmission, which is obviously of concern because that facilitates more rapid spread between a species.” While there are no registered vaccines for treating H5 bird flu in mammals, the United States has undertaken experimental trials on a small number of seals. The SA government said last week it was investigating potential opportunities to vaccinate high-priority at-risk mammals, such as Australian sea lions at Seal Bay on Kangaroo Island. The Australian Marine Conservation Society said the arrival of bird flu in SA followed significant environmental harm caused by the algal bloom. Campaigns director Alexia Wellbelove said some species, such as sea lions, were in poorer condition because their food sources had been affected, “meaning they are likely more vulnerable”. Wellbelove said the organisation had been calling for increased funding to target other threats to the species, such as fishing. “With reported mass mortality of terns and now the death of a long-nosed fur seal on the Pages it is now highly likely that this vital population of Australian sea lions has also been exposed to the virus,” she said. https://www.wdbo.com/news/world/exclusiv.text: Subscribe to WDBO newsletter(Opens a new window) WDBO facebook feed(Opens a new window) WDBO twitter feed(Opens a new window) WDBO instagram feed(Opens a new window) World AP Exclusive: US coaches Polish forces in a drone-focused drill based on lessons from Ukraine By KONSTANTIN TOROPIN, Associated Press August 30, 2026 at 8:25 pm EDT Enter Fullscreen Expand Germany US Ukraine Military Exercise US special forces patrol during a joint military exercise with forces from Poland at the Joint Multinational Readiness Center in Hohenfels near Nuernberg, Germany, Friday, Aug. 28, 2026. (AP Photo/Konstantin Toropin) (Konstantin Toropin/AP Photo/Konstantin Toropin) By KONSTANTIN TOROPIN, Associated Press August 30, 2026 at 8:25 pm EDT HOHENFELS, Germany — On a moonless and rainy night, a group of soldiers emerged from a ramshackle building meant to resemble a church. The alpine terrain loomed over them as they quietly set off for the tree line of the German countryside a short distance away. The soldiers are members of the Polish special forces and are taking part in an exercise designed only months ago that simulates moving through enemy lines, traversing miles of enemy territory and launching a drone strike on a key enemy location . Initially designed by the Army's Green Berets for U.S. special forces, the exercise that began Friday is informed by and simulates many of the challenges that Ukrainian troops have experienced in their conflict with Russia . It is the first time a NATO ally like Poland has undertaken the training, and it comes at a time when tensions between Russian President Vladimir Putin and NATO countries have escalated . “We’re using lessons learned from Ukraine,” an Army Green Beret officer assigned to the training complex said Thursday. “All of those effects that we’re seeing either Russia or Ukraine having to overcome — we’re doing our best to replicate.” The Associated Press received rare access to both the training ground and the troops conducting the exercise, which has only been conducted twice before, both times this year, by two different Green Beret teams. The drill highlights the focus that some parts of the U.S. military have on learning the latest techniques in drone warfare , pioneered by Ukraine during its 4 1/2-year effort to repel Russian forces. It also shows how the U.S., its NATO allies and Ukraine are working together to counter the threat of possible further Russian action in coming years even as the Trump administration has warned of troop drawdowns in Europe . CIA Director John Ratcliffe went to Moscow this week to warn Russia not to attack NATO countries, The Wall Street Journal reported . Russia has the appetite to conduct sabotage and cyberattacks against NATO countries, but Putin wants to avoid a direct confrontation , according to three Western officials, who spoke Friday on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military matters. How special forces are learning to sneak behind enemy lines to deploy drones During the exercise in Germany, a senior enlisted soldier familiar with the training scenario at Joint Multinational Readiness Center Hohenfels — about an hour's drive southeast from Nuremberg — said the plan is to run it several times a year. The officer said he expects most, if not all, of the 32 NATO nations to express interest in sending their troops to try the exercise. Both spoke on condition of anonymity in line with the U.S. military's longstanding policy of not publicly identifying individual members of special forces units. The scenario, which runs for several days, takes place on a large, 1,100-square-mile (3,000-square-kilometer) plot of land nestled in the Bavarian countryside. Poland's special forces will be expected to sneak past a U.S. Army airborne infantry unit, whose soldiers will play the enemy. The U.S. airborne infantry unit will parachute into the closed-off training area at the Army's Hohenfels base and set themselves up into a front line. Assuming the Polish forces can make their way past the U.S. Army, they must then move north — through about 60 miles (100 kilometers) of German countryside — to another training area in the town of Grafenwoehr, where they are expected to destroy a simulated target. In between lie German farms and villages, private and government cameras, as well as a city with a large population, all of which not only pose as obstacles but also create the potential for them to be spotted. The senior enlisted soldier said that in previous instances of the exercise, the Army Green Berets removed their uniforms “so they can blend in” before adding that “blend in also means don’t get seen by civilians.” German civilians in the area largely are not aware of the exercise and serve as a reasonable test of how well special forces can blend into the local population. If they fail, reports of suspicious people to police will make it back to the military, which will use them to pinpoint the team. “This is supposed to be Russia and you’re going to stand out in Russia,” the enlisted soldier added. Plus, the U.S. Army also will be looking for the Polish forces with drones of their own. If they're spotted, “now you have the entire Russian arsenal coming at you,” the enlisted soldier said. The U.S. Army can either send a military police unit to hunt for the Polish special forces with dogs or direct more drones to the area. In previous versions of the exercise, the U.S. Army had access to more than a hundred drones, the enlisted soldier said. Troops are able to be “captured or killed” as part of the training. Countries seek help from Ukraine on drone warfare While the exercise taps into drones and NATO teamwork, the message of collaboration and the value of drones has been somewhat mixed lately across the military. President Donald Trump stirred confusion among NATO allies by going back and forth on drawing down U.S. troop levels in Europe, and the administration has launched a force review on next steps. And last week, the Army's top officer shuttered a unit that specialized in drone warfare. But overall, there is growing interest in tapping Ukraine for its expertise on modern warfare and, specifically, drones. In March, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country was helping five countries in the Middle East and Gulf region counter Iranian drone attacks launched during the war with the United States, while the U.S. and European countries were among those requesting support. Meanwhile, the number of mysterious drone incursions in Europe have grown, including as recently as this month, when a pair of drones were spotted over a German military base and a drone carrying explosives was found at a key cargo airport in Germany. ___ Associated Press writer Emma Burrows in London contributed to this report. Photograph: Spokesperson for the President of the Republic of the Union of Myanmar/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Aung San Suu Kyi speaking on the phone to her son Kim Aris in Naypyidaw. Photograph: Spokesperson for the President of the Republic of the Union of Myanmar/AFP/Getty Images Aung San Suu Kyi Aung San Suu Kyi’s son speaks to detained former Myanmar leader for first time in five years Kim Aris says ‘hearing her voice again means more than words can express’ amid loosening of detention restrictions Agence France-Presse in Yangon Thu 22 Oct 2026 06.38 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The son of Myanmar ’s Aung San Suu Kyi has been allowed to speak to the detained former democratic leader for the first time in more than five years. “Today, I was finally able to speak with my mother, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi , after more than five years. Hearing her voice again means more than words can express,” Kim Aris said in a post on Facebook on Thursday. Aung San Suu Kyi is under house arrest in the capital, Naypyidaw, according to Myanmar authorities, where she has been sequestered since being unseated in a 2021 military coup . Myanmar’s ousted leader Aung San Suu Kyi seen in rare photos after receiving gift from King Charles Read more Images accompanying his Facebook post appeared to show Aris, who lives in the UK standing outside the Myanmar embassy in London. “I am deeply grateful to everyone who has stood by my mother and me. I believe your voices helped make this moment possible,” the post said. “But my mother is 81 and remains unjustly detained. One conversation is not regular family access.” Myanmar’s military held Aung San Suu Kyi, won the 1991 Nobel peace prize, in almost total seclusion for five years after the February 2021 coup, which ended a tentative decade-long experiment with democracy. But in recent months authorities have increasingly advertised the loosening of her detention and published photographs of her taking private meetings, as supporters have demanded “proof of life” of the octogenarian. On Monday, authorities said she received a package from Britain’s King Charles, including two books about soil and a “sealed diplomatic communication” from the monarch. Buckingham Palace did not comment on the contents of the communication. Myanmar authorities said Aung San Suu Kyi was moved from a prison in Naypyidaw to house arrest in April, and in August they published images of her meeting the nation’s Red Cross representative. After ruling Myanmar as military chief for five years, Min Aung Hlaing – who ousted Aung San Suu Kyi in the 2021 coup – was earlier this year installed as civilian president. Analysts described the election that put him in office as a charade, and said he could be loosening restrictions on Aung San Suu Kyi in an attempt to court international legitimacy. Africa Home page Africa 0 0 Events in Warsaw aimed to prevent Poland from becoming presidential republic - FM © APA | Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski 31 October 2026 15:18 (UTC +04:00) The events in Warsaw were aimed at preventing Poland from becoming a presidential republic, Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski said in a post on X, APA reports. "The events at the Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw last night were not elegant but the alternative was to concede an unconstitutional transformation of Poland into a presidential republic. Poland continues to be ruled by a coalition government elected by parliament," the minister stated. It should be noted that tensions arose at Poland's Constitutional Tribunal on October 30 over the management of the government and judicial system. Following the decision to suspend Tribunal President Bogdan Święczkowski from his position, a protest was held outside the building. Polish President Karol Nawrocki cut short his visit and returned to Warsaw, describing the events as a violation of the constitutional order. Sikorski had previously justified the police intervention by citing the need to restore the Tribunal's operations and allow judges elected by parliament to assume their duties.
